text: This is lesson ten, Chapter Two, Classic RL Algorithms. Monte Carlo is model-free, but it has to wait for an entire episode to finish before updating anything. Temporal difference learning fixes that: model-free, but it updates after every single step.

Here's the update. Instead of waiting for the full actual return like Monte Carlo does, TD zero uses just one real reward, plus the current estimated value of whatever state comes next. That combination is called the TD target, and subtracting the current value estimate from it gives the TD error — exactly how much that one step of evidence says the estimate should move.

This is called bootstrapping, because the target itself leans on the model's own current estimate of the next state's value, not on ground truth. It's an estimate helping to update another estimate. Dynamic programming bootstraps too, using a known model; TD bootstraps from one real, sampled step instead.

Here's a worked number. Say the current estimate is four, the observed reward is one, the next state's estimate is six, gamma is point nine, and alpha is point one. The TD target comes out to six point four, the TD error is two point four, and the new estimate nudges up to four point two four. That nudge happens again at every single step.

TD trades a bit of early bias for lower variance and the ability to update continuously, which is exactly why it became the foundation for the next two algorithms. Next up, lesson eleven: Q-learning, which applies this same TD idea to the action-value function, off-policy.
